summary: Defines Opus, an audio codec for interactive speech and music. It handles uses such as voice over IP, videoconferencing, in-game chat, and live music, and scales from low-bitrate narrowband speech up to very high quality stereo music. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Opus is a clever way to squeeze sound into small packages for sending over the internet. It works for a quiet whisper or a whole band, and it adjusts to how much room there is.

subtitle: One audio codec that stretches from thin-line voice calls to high-quality stereo music, switching modes on the fly.

tldr.problem: Interactive audio such as VoIP, videoconferencing, in-game chat and live music needs one codec that works at very different bitrates, bandwidths and delays, and can adapt to changing network conditions without renegotiating the session.
tldr.mechanism: Opus combines a linear-prediction layer (derived from SILK) that is efficient for low-frequency speech with an MDCT layer (derived from CELT) that is efficient for music and high frequencies. Either layer or both can be active, they share one range coder, and a one-byte table-of-contents header tells the decoder which configuration each packet uses.
tldr.outcome: The codec scales from 6 kbit/s narrowband mono speech to 510 kbit/s fullband stereo music. The decoder source code in Appendix A is the normative definition. RFC 6716 is a Proposed Standard that is updated by RFC 8251.

today: RFC 6716 is a Proposed Standard, and it is updated by RFC 8251. The RFC itself says the decoder source code in Appendix A is the normative definition.

sections.title: Two Layers, One Codec
sections.content:
RFC 6716 defines the Opus interactive speech and audio codec. It is built from a layer based on Linear Prediction (LP) and a layer based on the Modified Discrete Cosine Transform (MDCT). The reasoning in the introduction is that linear prediction codes low frequencies of speech more efficiently than transform techniques, while the situation is reversed for music and higher speech frequencies. A codec with both layers can operate over a wider range, and can reach better quality by combining them, than either layer alone.

The LP layer is based on the SILK codec and supports narrowband (NB), medium-band (MB) and wideband (WB) audio with frame sizes from 10 ms to 60 ms. The MDCT layer is based on the CELT codec and supports NB, WB, super-wideband (SWB) and fullband (FB) audio with frame sizes from 2.5 ms to 20 ms. A Hybrid mode uses both layers at once, with a 10 or 20 ms frame and SWB or FB bandwidth: the LP layer codes the low frequencies and the MDCT layer codes everything above 8 kHz.

Opus scales from 6 kbit/s narrowband mono speech to 510 kbit/s fullband stereo music, with algorithmic delays from 5 ms to 65.2 ms. It can switch between all of its modes without renegotiating the session. The encoder has control parameters such as bitrate, number of channels, audio bandwidth, frame duration, complexity, packet loss resilience, in-band forward error correction, constant or variable bitrate, and discontinuous transmission. They only affect the encoder, because their effect on the bitstream is signaled in-band, so any decoder can decode any Opus stream.

The primary normative part of the specification is the reference source code in Appendix A, and only its decoder portion is normative. The prose is there to explain the what and the why.
sections.eli5: Imagine two tools: one is great at drawing faces, the other at drawing landscapes. Opus carries both and uses whichever fits the picture, or both together. It picks the right one without stopping the conversation.

sections.title: Packets and the TOC Byte
sections.content:
An Opus encoder produces packets: contiguous sets of bytes meant to be sent as one unit. A packet may hold several audio frames as long as they share the operating mode, audio bandwidth, frame size and channel count. The framing is not self-delimiting: a lower layer such as UDP, RTP, Ogg or Matroska must say how long the packet is. A decoder MUST support this framing. A self-delimiting variant in Appendix B is OPTIONAL.

Every well-formed packet has at least one byte, the table-of-contents (TOC) byte. Its top five bits, config, select one of 32 configurations of mode, audio bandwidth and frame size. One bit, s, is 0 for mono and 1 for stereo. The last two bits, c, give the frame count code: 0 means one frame, 1 means two frames of equal compressed size, 2 means two frames of different sizes, and 3 means an arbitrary number of frames.

Lengths of frames in code 2 and code 3 packets use one or two bytes. A first byte of 0 means no frame (DTX or a lost packet), 1 to 251 is the length in bytes, and 252 to 255 means a second byte follows, giving a total of (second_byte*4)+first_byte. No single frame may exceed 1275 bytes. Code 3 packets add a frame count byte with a VBR flag, a padding flag and a frame count M, plus optional Opus padding that the encoder MUST set to zero to avoid creating a covert channel. A code 3 packet MUST NOT carry more than 120 ms of audio.

The RFC lists seven well-formedness rules, [R1] to [R7]. A receiver MUST NOT process packets that break them as normal Opus packets. They are reserved for future uses such as in-band headers, and an implementation of this specification may treat them as malformed and discard them.

Appendix B describes the self-delimiting variant, which adds one extra length field before the first frame. It is meant for cases like packing several one- or two-channel Opus streams into a multi-channel stream at the transport layer. Nothing in the packet lets a decoder tell the two framings apart, so the transport layer must establish which one is in use.
sections.eli5: Each Opus packet starts with a tiny label, like a sticker on a lunchbox that says what kind of food is inside and how many portions. The decoder reads the sticker first so it knows how to open the box.

sections.title: The Shared Range Coder
sections.content:
Both layers write their data with one range coder, an entropy coder closely related to arithmetic coding that works in bytes rather than bits. Using a single coder means there are no padding bits wasted between the layers. All of its arithmetic must be bit-exact integer arithmetic.

Each symbol is drawn from a finite alphabet with a static probability model, so contexts are not updated as symbols are decoded. A symbol is described by a tuple (fl, fh, ft) of 16-bit unsigned integers. The decoder keeps a two-value state, val and rng, both 32-bit unsigned. At initialization rng is 128, and the decoder renormalizes until rng is greater than 2**23. The reference code also has faster equivalents for common cases: a binary-symbol decoder and a table-based decoder using an inverse cumulative distribution table.

Some values, called raw bits, bypass the range coder and are packed backwards from the end of the frame. This makes them more resilient to bit errors and lowers complexity. Raw bits are used only in the CELT layer. If the range decoder consumes all the bytes of a frame it MUST keep using zeros when it needs more input.
sections.eli5: The range coder is like a very good packing machine. Common things get tiny labels and rare things get longer ones, so everything fits in the smallest possible bag.

sections.title: The SILK Layer for Speech
sections.content:
The LP layer uses a modified SILK codec. It runs an excitation signal through a long-term prediction (LTP) filter, used on voiced frames, and then a short-term prediction filter. Internally it runs at NB, MB or WB rates, and in Hybrid frames it still runs only at WB. The version in Opus is substantially modified from, and not compatible with, the stand-alone SILK codec that Skype used.

One Opus frame holds either a single 10 ms SILK frame or one to three 20 ms SILK frames, and a stereo frame can double that count to as many as six. Each SILK frame has two or four 5 ms subframes. Optional Low Bit-Rate Redundancy (LBRR) frames are reduced-bitrate copies of the previous audio that help recover from packet loss. They come first, before the regular frames. Packing several SILK frames in one Opus frame saves on average half a byte per SILK frame, because they all share one range coder.

Each frame carries its frame type, per-subframe quantization gains (coded on a 6-bit log scale), normalized Line Spectral Frequencies decoded through a two-stage vector quantizer (order 10 for NB and MB, order 16 for WB), pitch lags and LTP filter coefficients for voiced frames, a 2-bit seed for a pseudorandom generator, and finally the excitation. The excitation uses a modified Pyramid Vector Quantizer with a fixed dimension of 16, grouped into 16-sample shell blocks.

Stereo uses a variant of mid-side coding, so a mono decoder can decode just the mid channel. The decoder then predicts the side channel from the mid channel to unmix left and right, and finally resamples to the output rate. The resampler is not normative, but its minimum delay is.
sections.eli5: SILK works like a voice impersonator: it learns the shape of a person's throat and mouth, then only has to send the little buzz that drives it. That is much less data than sending the whole sound.

sections.title: The CELT Layer for Music and High Frequencies
sections.content:
The MDCT layer is based on CELT. It splits the spectrum into bands that roughly follow the Bark scale of the ear's critical bands. The normal layer uses 21 bands, and in Hybrid mode the first 17 (everything up to 8 kHz) are not coded. A band can hold from one to 176 MDCT bins per channel. In each band, the energy (gain) is coded separately from the shape, which makes it easy to preserve the spectral envelope. The unit-norm shape is coded with a Pyramid Vector Quantizer (PVQ).

Energy is coded in three steps: a coarse step with a fixed resolution of 6 dB, predicted from the previous frame and the previous bands, followed by two fine steps. A frame can be marked intra so that its energy is coded without reference to earlier frames.

The bit allocation is mostly implicit. The encoder and decoder both know the available bits from the packet size, so no codebook sizes need to be signaled. The decoder MUST recover this allocation exactly, because any deviation corrupts the output.

Transients are handled with several short MDCTs instead of one long one, and with per-band time-frequency resolution changes. An anti-collapse step inserts pseudo-random energy into bands that would otherwise drop to zero. For stereo, CELT can use mid-side, intensity or dual stereo. Tonal signals benefit from a pitch pre-filter in the encoder and a matching post-filter in the decoder, followed by de-emphasis.
sections.eli5: CELT is like describing a song by how loud each group of notes is and what shape they have, instead of writing down every sound. That works well for music and for the high squeaky parts of a voice.

sections.title: Loss Resilience and Concealment
sections.content:
Opus gives several tools for coping with packet loss. The encoder can adjust how much it depends on earlier frames, trading bitrate against error propagation. In-band Forward Error Correction (FEC) re-encodes perceptually important packets, such as onsets or transients, at a lower bitrate and adds them to a later packet. In the SILK layer this appears as the LBRR frames.

Packet Loss Concealment (PLC) is an optional decoder-side feature that SHOULD be included when receiving from an unreliable channel. It is not part of the bitstream, so many implementations are acceptable. In the reference decoder, CELT mode finds a periodicity in the signal and repeats the waveform at the pitch offset, while SILK mode extrapolates with linear prediction.

The RFC also treats clock drift. When the sender's clock runs slower than the receiver's, the effect resembles packet loss, and a receiver for live streams SHOULD conceal it, possibly by invoking the PLC. When the sender's clock is faster, the receiver MAY skip a packet entirely, which is likely to be less noticeable than dropping a frame after decoding it.
sections.eli5: If a few words go missing on a phone call, Opus can guess what was probably said, or use a rough backup copy it tucked into the next message. Either way the call keeps going smoothly.

sections.title: Switching Modes Mid-Stream
sections.content:
Switching between modes, bandwidths and channel counts needs care to avoid audible glitches. Some switches need no special handling because the MDCT overlap smooths them: any two CELT-only configurations, any two Hybrid configurations, and WB SILK to Hybrid. Hybrid to WB SILK needs the CELT overlap buffer added into the first SILK-only packet. Changing the channel count in SILK-only or Hybrid is smoothest if the encoder gradually varies the stereo width, and it SHOULD do so.

The hardest switches are those between the LP model and the MDCT model, and bandwidth changes inside SILK-only mode. To smooth them, an Opus frame may carry redundancy: an extra 5 ms CELT frame placed in the first Opus frame after the transition, or in the last one before it. SILK-only frames signal redundancy implicitly, if at least 17 bits remain after the SILK part. Hybrid frames signal it with a flag, only if at least 37 bits remain. One more flag says whether the redundant frame belongs at the start or the end of the frame.

Transitions with redundancy, and a few that need none, are normative, and PLC MUST NOT be applied during them unless there is real packet loss. Other transitions are non-normative: the recommended approach is to reset decoder state and use PLC to fill the gap. Encoders SHOULD NOT use redundancy in ways other than those the RFC illustrates. The decoder also resets its SILK state before every SILK-only or Hybrid frame that follows a CELT-only frame.
sections.eli5: It is like changing from walking to riding a bike without the rider falling off. Opus sends a tiny extra bit of sound around the change, so you do not hear a bump.

sections.title: Building an Opus Encoder
sections.content:
Unlike the decoder, an Opus encoder is not required to support every mode. A valid, if less than optimal, encoder may include only a SILK module or only a CELT module. In the reference encoder the application chooses the frame size, while the number of channels, bandwidth and mode are picked automatically (unless overridden) from the requested bitrate, input sampling rate, type of signal (speech or music) and frame size. The signal type currently has to be supplied by the application. When configured for VoIP, the encoder applies a second-order high-pass filter with a cut-off around 50 Hz.

The SILK encoder converts the sample rate, then for stereo input computes an adaptive mid-side representation, in which the side signal is predicted from the mid signal. The side channel is only sent when it has enough energy. The core encoder then runs voice activity detection, pitch analysis, noise shaping analysis, prediction analysis, LSF and LTP quantization, and a noise shaping quantizer. SILK was designed for VBR, but the reference implementation also has a CBR mode, which gives lower quality at a given average bitrate and costs more computation.

For CELT, most of the encoder follows directly from the decoder. The notable encoder-side decisions include band boost, allocation trim (a value from 0 to 10, with a default of 5), band skipping, the mid-side versus dual stereo choice, intensity stereo thresholds by bitrate, and a time-frequency resolution choice made with the Viterbi algorithm. The PVQ search in the reference encoder is a greedy search, and implementers MAY use any other search method.
sections.eli5: The decoder follows a recipe exactly. The encoder is the cook who can make smart choices, such as which pan to use, as long as the dish comes out in the form the recipe expects.

sections.title: Conformance and Test Vectors
sections.content:
Conformance is defined mainly through the reference decoder in Appendix A. If the prose and the source code disagree, the code takes precedence. A compliant decoder's output MUST be within the thresholds of the opus_compare tool when compared to the reference output for each test vector, for every output sampling rate and channel count it supports. It MUST also end with the same final range decoder state as the reference decoder. A decoder need not support every output sampling rate or channel count.

The test vectors are not included in the RFC because of size, but are available from the IETF 83 proceedings and the Opus website. The RFC gives their SHA1 hashes, for twelve test vectors. The test tool reports a quality metric, where 0 is the passing threshold and 100 is output identical to the reference. The threshold corresponds to additive white noise with a 48 dB signal-to-noise ratio, and the RFC RECOMMENDS a quality above 90 for 48 kHz decoding.

Appendix A holds the whole reference implementation in C, as base64 text that can be extracted with a shell command. Opus Custom is an OPTIONAL extension for unusual sample rates and frame sizes. It uses only the CELT layer, needs out-of-band signaling, and its use is discouraged for all but very special applications.
sections.eli5: To prove your player works, you play a set of official practice recordings and check that your answers match the official answers closely enough. If they do, you pass.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Opus should not be used with insecure ciphers or cipher modes that are vulnerable to known-plaintext attacks. The RFC points out that the zeros used in Opus padding, digital silence frames and the TOC byte can all produce predictable data.

Implementations need to be robust against malicious payloads. A decoder must not overrun its memory or spend excessive resources on a crafted packet, and the same holds for encoders, to protect transcoding gateways. The RFC says the reference implementation has no known buffer overflow or crafted packet that significantly increases CPU load.

One caveat concerns CPUs where denormalized floating-point operations are slow. Silence or near silence could then increase CPU load. Adding very small offsets to affected signals is RECOMMENDED on such architectures, or the hardware can be told to treat denormals as zero. The fixed-point reference implementation has no such issue. The reference implementation was tested with valid and randomly corrupted packets, random packets and a fuzzing encoder, all under Valgrind, with no errors reported.
sections.eli5: Because the codec opens packets that strangers send, it has to be careful. A sneaky packet must never make it crash or work itself to exhaustion.
